anchor.surface_text: 10.  She was the partner of Ömer Koç (Ö.K.), a farmer whom she married in a religious ceremony in 1976 and with whom she had six children.

facts.text: Ö.K. died on 10 September 2002 while he and the applicant had been making preparations for an official marriage ceremony.

anchor.surface_text: Ö.K. died on 10 September 2002. The applicant stated that on that date, while she and her partner had been making preparations for an official marriage ceremony, Ö.K. had died following an illness.

facts.text: On 11 September 2003 the applicant brought proceedings before the İslahiye District Court seeking recognition of her religious marriage and registration of her daughter Emine as Ö.K.'s daughter.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 11 September 2003 the applicant brought proceedings before the İslahiye District Court on her own behalf and on behalf of her daughter Emine seeking rectification of the entry concerning her in the civil status register.

facts.text: On 26 September 2003 the District Court refused to recognise the applicant's religious marriage but granted the request to enter Emine as Ö.K.'s daughter; the judgment became final as no appeal was lodged.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  In a judgment of 26 September 2003 the District Court refused the applicant's request concerning her religious marriage but granted the request for Emine to be entered in the register as Ö.K.'s daughter.

facts.text: The applicant requested the Hatay retirement pension fund (Bağ-Kur) to award her and her daughter a survivor's pension and health insurance based on Ö.K.'s entitlement; the fund refused.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On an unspecified date the applicant requested the Hatay retirement pension fund (“Bağ‑Kur”) to award her and her daughter Emine a survivor's pension and health insurance cover on the basis of her late partner's entitlement.

facts.text: On 20 February 2003 the applicant applied to the İslahiye Labour Court to set aside the pension fund's refusal; on 20 May 2003 the court ruled it had no jurisdiction and referred the case to the Hatay Labour Court.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 20 February 2003 the applicant applied to the İslahiye Labour Court to have that decision set aside. On 20 May 2003 the latter decided that it had no jurisdiction ratione loci and that the case should be heard by the Hatay Labour Court.

facts.text: On 21 January 2004 the Hatay Labour Court found the applicant's religious marriage was not legally recognised and denied her survivor's pension but granted her daughter Emine the right to claim pension and health insurance.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  In a judgment of 21 January 2004 the Hatay Labour Court, in a ruling based on the judgment of the İslahiye District Court, found that the applicant's marriage to Ö.K. had not been validated.

facts.text: On 10 February 2004 the applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, arguing her religious marriage and children should entitle her to pension and health insurance benefits.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  On 10 February 2004 the applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. She argued that the extract from the civil status register stated that she was the wife of Ö.K., who was registered in the village of Kerküt.

facts.text: On 3 June 2004 the Court of Cassation upheld the Hatay Labour Court's judgment rejecting the applicant's claim for survivor's pension and health insurance benefits.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  In a judgment of 3 June 2004, served on the applicant on 28 June 2004, the Court of Cassation upheld the impugned judgment.

facts.text: The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 December 2004, alleging inability to claim retirement benefits and health insurance due to non-recognition of her religious marriage.

anchor.surface_text: 1.  The case originated in an application (no. 3976/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Ms Şerife Yiğit (“the applicant”), on 6 December 2004.

facts.text: The applicant alleged that having lived in a religious marriage with her partner with whom she had six children, she was unable to claim retirement benefits or health insurance on his death in 2002, unlike the children.

anchor.surface_text: 3.  Relying on Article 8 of the Convention, the applicant alleged that, having lived in a “religious marriage” (imam nikâhı) with her partner, with whom she had six children, she had been unable to claim retirement benefits (survivor's pension) or health insurance (social security) cover on her partner's death in 2002, unlike the children born of the relationship, which was not recognised by the law or the national courts.

facts.text: The applicant and her children lived with Ö.K. until his death in 2002, constituting a family within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: It is not contested by the parties that the applicant and her children lived with Ö.K. until his death in 2002. The Court considers that it does not have jurisdiction to rule on the place or role of religious marriage in Turkish law and its social consequences. It simply notes that the applicant, Ö.K. and their children lived together in such a way that they constituted a 'family' within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention.

arguments.claim: The Government raised an objection of failure to exhaust domestic remedies, arguing the applicant had not appealed the District Court's refusal to recognise her religious marriage.

anchor.surface_text: failure to exhaust domestic remedies. They pointed out that the applicant had brought proceedings before the 3slahiye District Court seeking recognition of her religious marriage to her deceased partner. The action had been dismissed by the court and the applicant had not appealed against that decision to the Court of Cassation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court observed the applicant had pursued appropriate remedies before the Labour Court and Court of Cassation regarding survivor's pension claims, thus exhausting domestic remedies.

arguments.claim: The applicant maintained that she had exhausted domestic remedies by applying unsuccessfully to domestic courts for survivor's pension and social security benefits based on her partner's entitlement.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant maintained that she had exhausted domestic remedies, pointing out that she had applied unsuccessfully to the domestic courts for a survivor's pension and social security benefits based on her partner's entitlement.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court agreed the applicant had made normal use of available and effective domestic remedies before lodging the application with the Court.

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged that refusal to award survivor's pension and social security benefits based on her religious marriage constituted discrimination prohibited by Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: difference in treatment based on the non-civil nature of her marriage. The applicant complained that she had not been awarded a retirement pension and social security benefits based on her late partner's entitlement on discriminatory grounds for the purposes of Article 14 of the Convention.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the difference in treatment between religious and civil marriage was justified by the principle of secularism and the aim of protecting women and public order, including preventing polygamy.

anchor.surface_text: The Government began by pointing out that the regulation of marriage, which was compatible with Article 12 of the Convention, fell within the State's margin of appreciation. Civil marriage was clearly defined by the provisions of the Civil Code. Only persons who had contracted a civil marriage could enjoy the corresponding rights. That was why the applicant's application to the Hatay Labour Court seeking to benefit from her deceased partner's social security entitlements had been rejected on account of the absence of a civil marriage. Entitlement to a survivor's pension and social security benefits was not governed by the rules on inheritance laid down by the Civil Code. Under the domestic social security legislation, the lawful surviving partner of a civil marriage and his or her children could inherit such entitlement. Next, the Government stressed the importance of the principle of secularism, which was enshrined in the Constitution. It was not possible to attach legal consequences to the application of religious rules. The legislature's aim was to prevent religious marriages and protect the most important building-block of society, namely the family. As a secular State, Turkey did not recognise religious marriages. In a similar situation where the woman rather than the man was in employment, the latter would not be awarded a survivor's pension or social security benefits on her death. Religious marriage placed women at a disadvantage compared to men. In order to prevent discrimination and grant the same rights to women and men, the law required religious marriages to be preceded by a civil ceremony. The law governing civil marriage did not impose any particular restrictions on the right to marry, neither could the legislature oblige persons who were living together to marry in accordance with the Civil Code. In the Government's submission, the domestic authorities had not subjected the applicant to discriminatory treatment compared to other persons in a similar situation. There was no provision of domestic law which entitled a “surviving life companion” or “surviving partner” to receive a survivor's pension or social security benefits as the deceased's successor. The main difference between religious and civil marriage was that the former was not recognised by the law. Religious marriages were not registered. Persons wishing to enter into such a union were free to do so, but only after they had contracted a civil marriage. Article 230 of the Criminal Code made it a punishable offence to solemnise a religious marriage before the civil ceremony. The object of that provision was to protect women against polygamy. If religious marriages were to be considered lawful all the attendant religious consequences would have to be recognised, for instance the fact that a man could marry four women. The only means of preventing that was to promote civil marriage and not to attach rights to religious marriage. A further legal argument militated against religious marriage, namely the principle of presumption of paternity, which was based on the existence of a civil marriage. Furthermore, the recognition of a child by his or her father did not entail regularisation of the latter's religious marriage. The applicant had had the opportunity to contract a civil marriage in order to secure entitlement to a survivor's pension and social security benefits in the event of her partner's death. Lastly, the Government submitted that a distinction needed to be made between a claim for damages under private law and an application for a survivor's pension and other social security benefits under the rules of public law. Under the latter, entitlement to such benefits required the existence of a legal relationship. As religious marriage was not recognised the applicant could not legally claim a survivor's pension or social security benefits based on her late partner's entitlement. Granting such rights to persons living in religious marriages would be tantamount to encouraging religious marriage. Under domestic law, the introduction of a claim for damages did not depend on the persons concerned being related. Admittedly, the courts accepted that a fiancée or close friend who had cared for the deceased or a person who had suffered a loss of income as a result of the death could be awarded damages; however, in such situations Turkish law provided for compensation irrespective of the existence of a religious or civil marriage.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the State's margin of appreciation in regulating marriage and social security benefits, recognizing the legitimate aims of protecting public order and women's rights, and found the difference in treatment proportionate.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that she was unable to claim pension or health insurance benefits because her marriage was religious rather than civil, and that religious marriage was a social reality in Turkey.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant did not regard her application as tending towards the recognition of religious marriage or polygamy. The Civil Code recognised religious marriages provided that they were solemnised after a civil ceremony had been performed. While she was aware of the relevant provision of the Criminal Code, she had doubts as to its effectiveness. In her view, religious marriage was a social reality throughout Turkey. Furthermore, her situation could have been regularised on the basis of the amnesty laws which were enacted regularly with a view to ensuring that children born outside marriage could be entered in the civil status register.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant was aware of the need to regularise her relationship by civil marriage and that the difference in treatment was justified and proportionate.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the difference in treatment based on the non-civil nature of the applicant's marriage pursued legitimate aims of protecting public order and the rights and freedoms of others, including the principle of secularism and protection of women.

anchor.surface_text: difference in treatment based on the non-civil nature of her marriage. The Court accepts that the difference in treatment in question primarily pursued the legitimate aims of protecting public order and protecting the rights and freedoms of others.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the legitimate aims cited by the Government as objective and reasonable justifications for the difference in treatment.

arguments.claim: The Court found there was a reasonable relationship of proportionality between the refusal to award benefits to partners in religious marriages and the legitimate aim pursued, given the clear and accessible rules on civil marriage and the applicant's knowledge of the need to regularise her situation.

anchor.surface_text: difference in treatment based on the non-civil nature of her marriage. The Court accepts that the difference in treatment in question primarily pursued the legitimate aims of protecting public order and protecting the rights and freedoms of others.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted the applicant had a long period to contract a civil marriage and that the legal framework was clear, thus the difference in treatment was proportionate to the legitimate aims pursued.

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged a breach of her right to respect for family life under Article 8 due to non-recognition of her religious marriage affecting survivor's benefits.

anchor.surface_text: Relying on Article 8 of the Convention, the applicant alleged that, having lived in a “religious marriage” (imam nikâhı) with her partner, with whom she had six children, she had been unable to claim retirement benefits (survivor's pension) or health insurance (social security) cover on her partner's death in 2002, unlike the children born of the relationship, which was not recognised by the law or the national courts.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that Article 8 did not impose an obligation on States to adopt a special regime for couples living together without civil marriage.

anchor.surface_text: The Government agreed with the Chamber's conclusion, taking the view that Article 8 did not impose an obligation on the Contracting States to adopt a special regime for couples living together without having contracted a civil marriage.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court agreed there was no obligation under Article 8 to recognise religious marriages or provide special regimes for unmarried couples.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the applicant, her partner and their children lived together constituting a 'family' within the meaning of Article 8, but that the State did not interfere with their family life by not recognising the religious marriage for survivor's benefits.

anchor.surface_text: It is not contested by the parties that the applicant and her children lived with 3.K. until his death in 2002. The Court considers that it does not have jurisdiction to rule on the place or role of religious marriage in Turkish law and its social consequences. It simply notes that the applicant, 3.K. and their children lived together in such a way that they constituted a 'family' within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court recognized the existence of family life but found no interference by the State with that family life by refusing to recognise religious marriage for benefits.

arguments.claim: The Court concluded that Article 8 cannot be interpreted as imposing an obligation on the State to recognise religious marriage or grant survivor's benefits to partners in religious marriages.

anchor.surface_text: The Court therefore finds no appearance of interference by the State with the applicant's family life. Accordingly, the Court is of the view that Article 8 cannot be interpreted as imposing an obligation on the State to recognise religious marriage.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no violation of Article 8 as the State did not interfere with family life and was not obliged to recognise religious marriages for social security benefits.
